newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals--Japan market quiet while LME rallies.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals--Japan market quiet while LME rallies.

text.p: A surge in copper and aluminium prices on the London Metal Exchange dominated the attention of Japanese traders this week, although physical markets remained quiet and premiums were steady, traders said on Wednesday.
They generally expected further near-term gains in LME copper prices, which rallied almost 10 percent in the last three sessions, although they said the move was largely speculative in nature.
"It's rising because of the funds," said one source at a large trade house. "(The volatility) is a real nuisance."

LME benchmark three-month copper prices rallied on Tuesday to an intraday high of $2,232 a tonne, a level not seen since mid-June when Sumitomo Corp shocked the copper world by firing its former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka and blaming him for massive losses from rogue trades.

With the latest rally, the market has grabbed back half the nearly $1,000 loss in the copper price from early May, when rumours first swirled that something was amiss at Sumitomo, until mid-July, when prices hit a 2-1/2-year low of $1,745 in the aftermath of the Sumitomo announcement.

Recent rallies have been spurred by a widening backwardation on the LME and steady drawdowns in LME warehouse stocks, which dipped below 100,000 tonnes on Tuesday amid talk that as much as 300,000 tonnes of metal may be moving into stocks of China's central reserve authorities.

Several Japanese traders and analysts believed there were sizable non-LME stocks of copper, however, although they strongly doubted last week's report of a possible 500,000 tonne unreported hoard in Rotterdam.
"I think there's a large quantity somewhere," said one copper trader, who suspected it was linked to copper stocks thought to have been held by Hamanaka before he was fired.
He said the charts suggested copper could eventually reach the $2,400 to $2,500 level before the uptrend ran its course.
Copper's rally lifted aluminium prices in its wake, with LME three-month aluminium hitting a 2-1/2-month high and approaching the $1,500 a tonne mark in early Wednesday trade.
One Japanese aluminium trader said, however, that the recent surge in LME prices was not tempting Japanese end-users to alter their hand-to-mouth purchasing practices.

He added that Japan's premiums continued to hold steady, while price negotiations later this month for the first quarter of 1997 were expected to keep premiums near this quarter's level of about $62 a tonne over LME cash prices.
